newsitem.title: UK: U.S. economy contines to worry U.K. fund managers.
newsitem.headline: U.S. economy contines to worry U.K. fund managers.

text.p: Lingering worries about the U.S. economy's outlook continue to haunt fund managers and despite a booming Wall Street few are being tempted to put more money into shares there, according to a Reuter poll.

The survey of global asset managers shows that, for the moment, most are content to just tweak their portfolios, pushing a little more into East European bourses, some into the Pacific region or a little less in Japanese shares.
"We've slashed U.S. equities from 42 to 27 percent. Wall Street has just about had it. We're putting the money into cash," one fund manager said.
Many remain wary of the U.S. stock market, despite its surge this year, recently touching new highs, wondering how long before it ends in tears.
"We will stay underweight in U.S. equities. We expect a slowdown in the economy in which favourable corporate earnings will dwindle," another manager said.
The poll shows that the average allocation for the U.S. stock market has barely moved for past three months.

Another manager said that for U.S. companies in such fields as telecommunications, health and technology the prospects were rosier, even with the chance that the Federal Reserve might nudge interest rates higher.
"There's really no need to raise U.S. interest rates and even if they do, it will only be quarter of a point," she said.
But she, and several others, was less bullish about the main Japanese stock market index except for those firms, such as retailers, likely to benefit from economic recovery.
"Japan is looking less comfortable," said ING Barings strategist Matthew Merrit who saw a somewhat cloudy outlook for the Nikkei index.
However, a number continue to be overweight in the rest of Asia.
Fleming Investment Management head of research Neil Honebon said if there was only a small move in U.S. rates, the region was unlikely to feel any knock-on impact.
However, he saw the U.S. economy as more likely to slowdown which meant little or no pressure on bond yields there which could even look cheap.
One fund manager said, however, there was still a tendency on bonds to go for the high-yield assets.
Several remained bullish about Eastern Europe shares, especially in Poland and Hungary, and Latin America.
